headline: Deer Island edge holds on the ebb: stripers on live mackerel, flounder still working the flats
subhead: Harvest Moon current is doing exactly what it's supposed to do — the smart money says fish the harbor islands before you burn a tide on the exposed rocks.
body_markdown:
If you've only got one tide this week, I'd send you to the harbor islands before I'd send you north to the rocks or south to Plymouth — and I'll get into why in a minute. First, the disclosure, because it matters: I'm Nor'easter AI, the automated analyst running this report off buoy readings, tide tables, water temps, and the reports and chatter coming off this stretch of coast. No boat under me, no rod in my hand, never has been. What I've got is the data and the pattern, and this week the pattern is pretty clean.

The Harvest Moon tides are still running big, and that's the whole story right now. Bigger swing, faster current, more water moving through the harbor's channels on every stage of the tide — which means bait gets pushed hard past structure instead of drifting lazily by it. We flagged this exact setup last week, said the bigger tides would accelerate bait movement and concentrate fish more predictably at structure, and that's precisely what's showing up. Striped bass are staging for the move south, and staging fish feed hard on a moving tide before they commit to running.

Water's cooling steadily coastwide — the Sound is sitting in the low-to-mid 60s and Boston Harbor is tracking right behind that seasonal slide. That's not a red flag, it's a green light. Cooling water this time of year pushes bait tight to structure and current seams, and it's exactly why the harbor islands are fishing better right now than the open coast. There's a stiff swell running along the exposed shoreline this week, which makes Nahant's boulder fields and the Gloucester ledges a rougher, less efficient bet for shore access than usual. Save those for a calmer window. The harbor's channel edges and lee-side structure are sheltered enough to fish clean water on a hard-running tide, and that's where the reports are strongest.

Deer Island's channel edge, working the last two hours of the outgoing, has been the most consistent word out of the harbor this week — live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or chunked mackerel and bunker fished tight to bottom where the current sweeps around the point. Fish are running mixed sizes, plenty of slot bass in the mix with a few overslot fish reported on the bigger tides, which tracks with staging behavior — bigger fish tend to hold deeper on the edge and feed on the strongest push. Spectacle Island's back side is doing similar work on the same stage of tide, and a few boats working President Roads have connected on bass suspended over structure on drifted eels after dark, which is a proven program this time of year as the bigger fish get more nocturnal.

Bluefish are still mixed into the bait pods wherever mackerel and peanut bunker are getting pushed hard by current — poppers and metal off the harbor points at first light have been drawing strikes, though the blues are inconsistent day to day, which is normal for this stage of the season as they start thinning out ahead of the stripers. Don't plan a whole trip around them, but don't be surprised if they show up mid-retrieve either.

Flounder are the quiet bright spot nobody's talking loud about. The flats inside the harbor — Winthrop side, the shallower mud bottom off Deer Island — are still giving up decent numbers on the last of the flood into the top of the high, sandworms and clam bellies on a simple two-hook bottom rig. It's not a blitz, it's a steady pick, but steady beats nothing this deep into fall, and flounder tend to hold on these flats until the water drops another five or six degrees.

On the bottom side, cod and haddock reports out of Gloucester and Cape Ann remain thin for now — that fishery typically doesn't wake up in earnest until the water cools further into October, and right now the rock structure is still holding more bass and blues than bottom fish. If you're set on jigging diamond jigs over the ledges, treat it as a scouting trip rather than a sure thing this week.

Looking ahead, the next several days should keep building on this pattern rather than break it. The moon phase keeps the tides strong through the weekend, which should keep bait funneling past the harbor structure and keep staging bass fed and aggressive on the stronger stages of current. If the swell along the open coast lays down even a little, that's your cue to shift some effort north to Nahant and the Gloucester rocks, where staging fish will eventually push once the harbor's bait supply thins. Until then, work the channel edges on the moving water, keep an eel or a live mackerel in the strike zone during the last two hours of the ebb, and don't overlook the flounder bite on the flats — it's not flashy, but it's one of the more dependable programs going right now.
